title: The Printing Press and the Spread of Ideas
subject: hist
paras: Before the middle of the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand. Scribes, many of them monks, could spend months producing a single volume, and the finished book was so expensive that only churches, universities, and the very wealthy could own one. As a result, written knowledge moved slowly, and errors crept into texts each time they were copied.

Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg, a metalworker in the German city of Mainz, developed a printing system that combined several existing technologies. The most important element was movable type: individual metal letters, cast in identical copies, that could be arranged into lines, inked, printed, and then reused for a different page. Gutenberg also adapted the screw press, already used to make wine and olive oil, and he developed an oil-based ink that stuck well to metal.

The results were dramatic. A print shop could produce hundreds of identical copies of a text in the time a scribe needed to make one. By 1500, presses were operating in more than two hundred European cities, and historians estimate that millions of books had been printed. Prices fell sharply, and for the first time, people of modest means such as merchants and craftsmen could afford to buy books.

Printing changed not only how many books existed but also what they contained. Because every copy of an edition was the same, scholars in different countries could refer to the same page and compare their work. Printers also began to publish in local languages rather than only in Latin, which helped standardize spelling and grammar in languages such as German and English.

The press also allowed new ideas to spread faster than authorities could control them. When Martin Luther criticized the Church in 1517, his arguments were printed and distributed across Germany within weeks. Some historians argue that the Reformation could not have succeeded without the press. Others caution that printing was a tool rather than a cause: it amplified movements that already had strong social and political roots.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, which of the following was a problem with hand-copied books?
opts: They were written only in local languages.
Mistakes were introduced each time a text was copied.
They could not be stored in universities.
They were printed on poor paper.
qs.why: errors crept into texts each time they were copied.

qs.q: The word "identical" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
opts: exactly alike
very large
carefully decorated
easily broken
qs.why: identical copies 即完全相同的副本。

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, Gutenberg's system included all of the following EXCEPT
opts: movable metal type
an adapted screw press
an oil-based ink
a machine that made paper
qs.why: 文中只提到 movable type、screw press 和 oil-based ink，没有造纸机。

qs.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about books before 1450?
opts: Merchants and craftsmen usually could not afford them.
They were cheaper than printed books.
They were produced in more than two hundred cities.
They were all written by Gutenberg.
qs.why: for the first time, people of modest means… could afford to buy books —— 说明此前买不起。

qs.q: Why does the author mention that scholars "could refer to the same page" in paragraph 4?
opts: To illustrate how uniform copies made scholarly comparison easier
To criticize scholars for copying one another
To explain why Latin disappeared
To show that books had become longer
qs.why: Because every copy of an edition was the same… compare their work.

qs.q: The word "it" in paragraph 5 ("it amplified movements") refers to
opts: the Church
the Reformation
printing
Germany
qs.why: printing was a tool rather than a cause: it amplified… —— it 指 printing。

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the view of the historians mentioned at the end of paragraph 5?
opts: The press was the only cause of the Reformation.
The press strengthened a movement that had other important causes.
The press had no effect on the Reformation.
Luther opposed the use of printing.
qs.why: printing was a tool rather than a cause… movements that already had strong… roots。

qs.q: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas of the passage. Introductory sentence: Gutenberg's printing press transformed the way knowledge spread in Europe.
opts: By combining movable type, a screw press, and new ink, Gutenberg made it possible to produce many copies quickly.
Many scribes were monks.
Printing made books far cheaper and more widely available.
Identical editions and printing in local languages changed scholarship and helped standardize languages.
Wine and olive oil were made with screw presses.
Luther lived in the city of Mainz.
qs.why: B、E 是细节；F 与原文不符。
